claim: Without synaptic stimulation, most AMPARs recycled in dynamin-independent endosomes containing the GTPase, Arf6.
source: Without synaptic stimulation, most AMPARs recycled in dynamin-independent endosomes containing the GTPase, Arf6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing co-localization between AMPARs and Arf6, and by data showing that dynasore treatment (which blocks dynamin) does not significantly affect AMPAR endocytosis.

claim: Few AMPARs recycled in dynamin-dependent endosomes labeled by transferrin receptors (TfRs) under constitutive conditions.
source: Few AMPARs recycled in dynamin-dependent endosomes labeled by transferrin receptors (TfRs).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing only 4-6% co-localization between endogenous GluA1 and TfR in dendrites under constitutive conditions.

claim: AMPAR recycling was blocked by alterations in the GTPase, TC10, which co-localized with Arf6 endosomes.
source: AMPAR recycling was blocked by alterations in the GTPase, TC10, which co-localized with Arf6 endosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that TC10 mutants reduced AMPAR surface levels and that TC10 co-localized with Arf6 endosomes (PCC = 0.77).

claim: TC10 mutants that reduced AMPAR recycling had no effect on increased AMPAR levels with long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: TC10 mutants that reduced AMPAR recycling had no effect on increased AMPAR levels with long-term potentiation (LTP)
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that neurons expressing TC10DN or TC10CA showed increased AMPAR surface/total ratios with cLTP similar to or greater than controls.

claim: TC10 mutants had little effect on decreased AMPAR levels with long-term depression.
source: TC10 mutants that reduced AMPAR recycling had no effect on increased AMPAR levels with long-term potentiation (LTP) and little effect on decreased AMPAR levels with long-term depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that TC10DN reduced cLTD-induced decrease by half, while TC10CA did not alter the cLTD-induced decrease.

claim: Internalized AMPAR levels in TfR-containing recycling endosomes increased after LTP.
source: However, internalized AMPAR levels in TfR-containing recycling endosomes increased after LTP, indicating increased AMPAR recycling through the dynamin-dependent pathway with synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that co-localization of internalized GluA1 with TfR increased from 21% to 56% after cLTP.

claim: LTP-induced AMPAR endocytosis is inconsistent with local recycling as a source of increased surface receptors.
source: LTP-induced AMPAR endocytosis is inconsistent with local recycling as a source of increased surface receptors, suggesting AMPARs are trafficked from other sites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that AMPAR endocytosis increases during LTP, which contradicts the prediction of the local recycling model that endocytosis should remain unchanged during LTP.

claim: Changes in glutamatergic synaptic strength in brain are dependent on AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) recycling.
source: Changes in glutamatergic synaptic strength in brain are dependent on AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) recycling, which is assumed to occur through a single local pathway.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific consensus about the role of AMPAR recycling in synaptic plasticity.

claim: AMPAR recycling was previously assumed to occur through a single local pathway.
source: Changes in glutamatergic synaptic strength in brain are dependent on AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPAR) recycling, which is assumed to occur through a single local pathway.
evidence: This claim references the prevailing assumption in the field prior to this study.

claim: NMDA- and AMPA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs/AMPARs) are the major excitatory synaptic receptors in brain.
source: NMDA- and AMPA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs/AMPARs) are the major excitatory synaptic receptors in brain.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about glutamate receptors.

claim: NMDARs and AMPARs are held at post-synaptic densities (PSDs) by scaffold proteins aligning the receptors with the presynaptic glutamate release sites.
source: They are held at post-synaptic densities (PSDs) by scaffold proteins aligning the receptors with the presynaptic glutamate release sites.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about receptor organization at synapses.

claim: Changes in synaptic strength, such as long-term potentiation (LTP), long-term depression (LTD), and homeostatic plasticity, largely reflect the number of functional synaptic AMPARs.
source: Changes in synaptic strength, such as long-term potentiation (LTP), long-term depression (LTD) (Malinow and Malenka, 2002), and homeostatic plasticity (Pérez-Otaño and Ehlers, 2005), largely reflect the number of functional synaptic AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Malinow and Malenka (2002) and Pérez-Otaño and Ehlers (2005).

claim: AMPAR internalization and recycling regulates AMPAR levels at synapses.
source: AMPAR internalization and recycling regulates AMPAR levels at synapses.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about AMPAR trafficking.

claim: Diffusion of extrasynaptic AMPARs outside PSDs, association and dissociation of AMPARs with PSDs, and the number of 'slots' that AMPAR can occupy in PSDs also contribute to setting AMPAR levels at PSDs.
source: Other processes, including diffusion of extrasynaptic AMPARs outside PSDs, association and dissociation of AMPARs with PSDs, and the number of 'slots' that AMPAR can occupy in PSDs (Malinow and Malenka, 2002; Ehlers, 2000; Lin et al., 2000; Petrini et al., 2009; Ehlers et al., 2007), also contribute to setting AMPAR levels at PSDs (Opazo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: During synaptic stimulation, 'constitutive' AMPAR recycling is increased several fold to become 'activity-dependent' AMPAR recycling.
source: During synaptic stimulation, 'constitutive' AMPAR recycling is increased several fold to become 'activity-dependent' AMPAR recycling (Ehlers, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ehlers (2000).

claim: AMPARs undergo endocytosis through clathrin-coated pits during activity-dependent recycling.
source: AMPARs undergo endocytosis through clathrin-coated pits during activity-dependent recycling (Carroll et al., 1999; Lüscher et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carroll et al. (1999) and Lüscher et al. (1999).

claim: Before exocytosis, AMPARs traffic through the recycling endosomes (REs) identified by co-localization with transferrin receptors (TfRs) and Rab11.
source: and before exocytosis, traffic through the recycling endosomes (REs) identified by co-localization with transferrin receptors (TfRs) (Ehlers, 2000) and Rab11 (Park et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ehlers (2000) and Park et al. (2004).

claim: During LTP, REs move from the dendritic shaft into synaptic spines from which regulated exocytosis of AMPARs appears to occur.
source: During LTP, REs move from the dendritic shaft into synaptic spines (Park et al., 2006) from which regulated exocytosis of AMPARs appears to occur.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al. (2006).

claim: It is uncertain whether AMPARs are exocytosed outside of the spines and traffic to PSDs via lateral diffusion or are exocytosed at specific sites near PSDs.
source: It is uncertain whether AMPARs are exocytosed outside of the spines and traffic to PSDs via lateral diffusion (Ashby et al., 2006; Yudowski et al., 2007; Tao-Cheng et al., 2011; Malinow and Malenka, 2002) or are exocytosed at specific sites near PSDs (Mohanasundaram and Shanmugam, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies presenting different possibilities.

claim: A minimal model of AMPAR constitutive and activity-dependent recycling assumes a single recycling pathway that starts at clathrin-coated pits, moves through REs, and ends with exocytosis back at the plasma membrane.
source: A minimal model of AMPAR constitutive and activity-dependent recycling has emerged from these and other studies. First, a single recycling pathway is assumed that starts at clathrin-coated pits (Blanpied et al., 2002), moves through REs, and ends with exocytosis back at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citation to Blanpied et al. (2002).

claim: The minimal model assumes that AMPAR recycling occurs locally, that is, AMPAR endocytosis and exocytosis occur at sites within the same synaptic domain.
source: Second, it is assumed that AMPAR recycling occurs locally, that is, AMPAR endocytosis and exocytosis occur at sites within the same synaptic domain.
evidence: This claim describes an assumption of the prevailing model in the field.

claim: The model predicts that during LTD, AMPAR levels in recycling endosomes and/or lysosomes at PSDs increase because endocytosis increases without increasing exocytosis from REs.
source: The model predicts that during LTD-AMPAR levels in recycling, endosomes and/or lysosomes at PSDs increase because endocytosis increases without increasing exocytosis from REs (Ehlers, 2000; Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a prediction of the prevailing model, supported by citations to Ehlers (2000) and Fernández-Monreal et al. (2012).

claim: During LTP, endocytosis is unchanged and AMPAR levels at PSDs are predicted to increase because of their exocytosis from REs causing decreased levels of AMPARs in REs.
source: During LTP, endocytosis is unchanged and AMPAR levels at PSDs are predicted to increase because of their exocytosis from REs causing decreased levels of AMPARs in REs (Park et al., 2006; Groc and Choquet, 2006).
evidence: This claim describes a prediction of the prevailing model, supported by citations to Park et al. (2006) and Groc and Choquet (2006).

claim: Many factors specifically affect AMPAR activity-dependent recycling without affecting constitutive recycling, such as AP2 and Brag2.
source: Many factors specifically affect AMPAR activity-dependent recycling without affecting constitutive recycling [e.g., AP2 (Lee et al., 2002), Brag2 (Scholz et al., 2010)]
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al. (2002) and Scholz et al. (2010).

claim: Some factors affect constitutive recycling without affecting activity-dependent recycling, such as NSF and PIP3.
source: and vice versa [e.g., NSF (Lee et al., 2002), PIP3 (Arendt et al., 2010)].
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al. (2002) and Arendt et al. (2010).

claim: AMPAR activity-dependent recycling is uncoupled from constitutive recycling and separate processes underlie the two types of AMPAR recycling.
source: These studies suggest that AMPAR activity-dependent recycling is uncoupled from constitutive recycling and that separate processes underlie the two types of AMPAR recycling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of various factors on activity-dependent vs. constitutive recycling.

claim: Transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins (TARPs), such as stargazin, interact with recycling AMPARs at synapses.
source: Transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins (TARPs), such as stargazin, interact with recycling AMPARs at synapses (Tomita et al., 2004; Neudauer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tomita et al. (2004) and Neudauer et al. (1998).

claim: TARPs interact with neuronal isoform of PDZ-protein interacting specifically with TC10 (nPIST).
source: TARPs interact with neuronal isoform of PDZ-protein interacting specifically with TC10 (nPIST) (Cuadra et al., 2004), suggesting that the Rho small G protein, TC10, might be a regulator of AMPAR recycling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cuadra et al. (2004).

claim: TC10 knockdown reduced endogenous TC10 mRNA by 90% in cortical neurons.
source: Using real-time PCR, we observed that endogenous TC10 mRNA was reduced by 90% in cortical neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of cell surface to total mCherry-GluA1 was similar from neuron to neuron (SEM = 14%).
source: We found that the ratio of cell surface to total mCherry-GluA1 was similar from neuron to neuron (SEM = 14%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of surface/total ratios.

claim: TC10 knockdown significantly reduced the surface/total mCherry-GluA1 ratio by 79% compared to control neurons.
source: With the TC10 knockdown, the surface/total mCherry-GluA1 ratio for neurons was significantly reduced by 79% (Figure 1A,D) compared to control neurons that expressed GFP without the shRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,D comparing TC10 knockdown to control.

claim: TC10DN and TC10CA mutants reduced GluA1-containing AMPAR surface levels by approximately 50% at somata.
source: Expression of wild-type TC10 (TC10WT) did not significantly alter surface levels at somata assayed by mCherry-GluA1 transfection, whereas TC10DN and TC10CA mutants reduced GluA1-containing AMPAR surface levels by ∼50% (Figure 1A,B; statistical details in the legend; images of the corresponding whole neurons are displayed in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TC10 knockdown with shRNA did not alter somata morphology, but dendritic morphology was altered and synapse numbers reduced.
source: While TC10 knockdown with shRNA did not alter somata morphology, dendritic morphology was altered and synapse numbers reduced (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on observations not shown in the manuscript.

claim: TC10DN, TC10CA mutants, and TC10WT did not alter dendrite morphology or synapse number.
source: In contrast, TC10DN, TC10CA mutants, and TC10WT did not alter dendrite morphology (not shown) or synapse number (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and observations not shown.

claim: In dendrites, GluA1 surface levels were reduced approximately 50% by TC10DN and TC10CA.
source: In dendrites, GluA1 surface levels were again reduced ∼50% by TC10DN and TC10CA
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring surface levels in dendrites.

claim: TC10WT expression caused a small but significant increase of GluA1 surface levels (33% ± 10%) in dendrites.
source: and a small but significant increase of GluA1 surface levels (33% ± 10%) was observed with TC10WT expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TC10DN and TC10CA reduced the synaptic AMPAR EPSC amplitudes by approximately 60%.
source: TC10DN and TC10CA reduced the synaptic AMPAR EPSC amplitudes by ∼60% (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: The number of functional AMPARs at synapses was reduced to approximately the same extent as the total number of AMPARs on the cell surface.
source: Thus, the number of functional AMPARs at synapses was reduced to approximately the same extent as the total number of AMPARs on the cell surface as measured by immunostaining.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparing the electrophysiology results with the immunofluorescence results.

claim: Expression of TC10DN and TC10CA in neurons caused the same effects on AMPAR levels, consistent with previous studies showing that the TC10 GTPase hydrolysis cycle is required for secretion.
source: Our findings with immunofluorescence and electrophysiology that expression of TC10DN and TC10CA in neurons caused the same effects on AMPAR levels in neurons are consistent with previous studies characterizing the role of TC10 in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This claim draws on inference from the current data and comparison with previous studies on TC10 function.

claim: Both TC10DN and TC10CA reduced depolarization-induced secretion of neuropeptide Y (NPY) in PC12 cells in the range of 40–60%.
source: Assaying depolarization-induced secretion of neuropeptide Y (NPY) in PC12 cells, both TC10DN and TC10CA reduced secretion in the range of 40–60% (Kawase et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawase et al. (2006).

claim: TC10WT reduced synaptic currents by 51% in paired whole-cell recordings from synaptically coupled cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, in the paired whole-cell recordings from synaptically coupled cultured hippocampal neurons, TC10WT reduced synaptic currents by 51% (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: TC10WT increased cell-surface AMPARs by 33% even though it reduced synaptic currents by 51%.
source: even though TC10WT increased cell-surface AMPARs by 33% (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The differential effect of TC10WT suggests that TC10 function somehow distinguishes between AMPAR trafficking to and/or from synaptic sites compared to other sites on the cell surface of dendrites.
source: This differential effect of TC10WT suggests that TC10 function somehow distinguishes between AMPAR trafficking to and/or from synaptic sites compared to other sites on the cell surface of dendrites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TC10WT on synaptic vs. dendritic surface AMPARs.

claim: Lentiviral infection of approximately 90% of the cultured neurons with TC10WT or the TC10 mutants did not alter endogenous GluA1 subunit levels.
source: Lentiviral infection of ∼90% of the cultured neurons with TC10WT or the TC10 mutants did not alter endogenous GluA1 subunit levels, indicating that TC10 mutants do not alter AMPAR subunit synthesis or degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: TC10 mutant expression did not appear to alter AMPAR trafficking through the secretory pathway in the soma.
source: Nor did the TC10 mutant expression appear to alter AMPAR trafficking through the secretory pathway in the soma (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: TC10WT, TC10DN, and TC10CA all strongly co-localized with the Golgi marker GM130 in somata.
source: Consistent with this possibility, TC10WT, TC10DN, and TC10CA all strongly co-localized with the Golgi marker GM130 in somata (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Little mCherry-GluA1 was found in the Golgi, and most GluA1 subunits co-localized with endoplasmic reticulum (ER) markers.
source: However, little mCherry-GluA1 was found in the Golgi, and most GluA1 subunits co-localized with endoplasmic reticulum (ER) markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), as previously observed for newly synthesized AMPAR subunits (Greger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and citation to Greger et al. (2002).

claim: The small amount of mCherry-GluA1 that co-localized with the Golgi marker did not significantly change with TC10DN and TC10CA expression compared to that of TC10WT.
source: The small amount of mCherry-GluA1 that co-localized with the Golgi marker did not significantly change with TC10DN and TC10CA expression compared to that of TC10WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B.

claim: When TC10 mutants were expressed, there was a significant increase in mCherry-GluA1 levels in the shafts of dendrites.
source: In fact, when TC10 mutants were expressed, there was a significant increase in mCherry-GluA1 levels in the shafts of dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C), suggesting that the TC10 mutants cause an accumulation of AMPAR intracellular levels in the dendritic shafts, but not in the somata, that results in the decreases in surface levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C.

claim: AMPARs enter REs in dendritic shafts after synaptic stimulation with AMPA or NMDA.
source: It is well established that AMPARs enter REs in dendritic shafts after synaptic stimulation with AMPA or NMDA (Malinow and Malenka, 2002; Newpher and Ehlers, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malinow and Malenka (2002) and Newpher and Ehlers (2008).

claim: There was little co-localization (4–6%) between endogenous GluA1 and TfR in dendrites under constitutive conditions.
source: Surprisingly, there was little co-localization, (4–6%), between endogenous GluA1 and TfR in dendrites under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization measurements.

claim: The percentage of co-localization between GluA1 and TfR did not change for non-transfected neurons or for neurons expressing Venus-tagged TC10WT, TC10DN, or TC10CA.
source: The percentage of co-localization did not change for non-transfected neurons or for neurons expressing Venus-tagged TC10WT, TC10DN, or TC10CA (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: TC10WT, TC10DN, or TC10CA expression did not alter the distribution of TfRs in the dendrites and did not significantly affect the recycling of TfRs.
source: TC10WT, TC10DN, or TC10CA expression also did not alter the distribution of TfRs in the dendrites and did not significantly affect the recycling of TfRs (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: There was significant co-localization between mCherry-tagged Rab11 and TfRs confirming that TfRs are largely in REs in dendrites.
source: To confirm the validity of TfRs as a recycling endosome marker, we tested another recycling endosome protein, Rab11, and found significant co-localization between mCherry-tagged Rab11 and TfRs confirming that TfRs are largely in REs in dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significantly higher degree of overlap (Pearson's correlation coefficient, PCC = 0.46) between endogenous GluA1 subunits and transfected HA-Arf6 compared to the approximately 5% co-localization observed between GluA1 and TfR puncta.
source: In contrast to the ∼5% co-localization observed between GluA1 and TfR puncta, we observed a significantly higher degree of overlap (Pearson's correlation coefficient, PCC = 0.46) between endogenous GluA1 subunits and transfected HA-Arf6 (Figure 2C,D), an established marker of endosomes in the Arf6, clathrin-independent pathway (Donaldson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2C,D and citation to Donaldson et al. (2009).

claim: There was a high degree of co-localization between TC10WT and HA-Arf6 (PCC = 0.77), indicating that TC10 is largely found in Arf6 endosomes in dendrites.
source: Importantly, there was a high degree of co-localization between TC10WT and HA-Arf6 (PCC = 0.77), indicating that TC10 is largely found in Arf6 endosomes in dendrites (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TC10DN significantly increased GluA1 co-localization with Arf6, changing from a PCC of 0.46 to 0.66.
source: TC10DN significantly increased GluA1 co-localization with Arf6, changing from a PCC of 0.46 to 0.66 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Increases in AMPARs co-localizing with Arf6 appeared to be at subdomains within Arf6 endosomes, consistent with TC10CA blocking AMPAR exit, and their accumulation in Arf6-endosomes.
source: Increases in AMPARs co-localizing with Arf6 appeared to be at subdomains within Arf6 endosomes (Figure 2C), consistent with TC10CA blocking AMPAR exit, and their accumulation in Arf6-endosomes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the co-localization pattern shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TC10CA caused GluA1 co-localization with Arf6 to significantly decrease from a PCC of 0.46 to 0.31, consistent with increased AMPAR exit from Arf6 endosomes.
source: The TC10CA mutant had the opposite effect. TC10CA caused GluA1 co-localization with Arf6 to significantly decrease from a PCC of 0.46 to 0.31, consistent with increased AMPAR exit from Arf6 endosomes (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2C,D and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Expression of TC10CA changed the size and number of the GluA1-containing puncta in dendritic shafts, with an increased number of smaller puncta and a loss of most of the larger puncta.
source: Expression of TC10CA changed the size and number of the GluA1-containing puncta in dendritic shafts. GluA1-containing puncta were much more numerous compared to TC10WT, with an increased number of smaller puncta and a loss of most of the larger puncta in dendrites (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by puncta analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AMPARs exiting from Arf6 endosomes remained in smaller transport vesicles because TC10CA blocked their exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
source: This result suggests that the AMPARs exiting from Arf6 endosomes remained in smaller transport vesicles because TC10CA blocked their exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of increased smaller puncta with TC10CA expression.

claim: The clathrin-dependent endocytosis pathway taken by TfRs requires dynamin function, while Arf6-dependent clathrin-independent endocytosis is independent of dynamin function.
source: The clathrin-dependent endocytosis pathway taken by TfRs requires dynamin function, while Arf6-dependent clathrin-independent endocytosis is independent of dynamin function (Doherty and McMahon, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doherty and McMahon (2009).

claim: Dynasore treatment caused TfRs to buildup at the plasma membrane.
source: Consistent with a block of its endocytosis, dynasore treatment appeared to cause TfRs to buildup at the plasma membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tf-Alexa 647 uptake was inhibited by 70% ± 18% in the presence of dynasore.
source: Tf-Alexa 647 uptake was inhibited by 70% ± 18% in the presence of dynasore (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Dynasore treatment did not significantly alter the levels or distribution of internalized mCherry-GluA1 subunits.
source: However, dynasore treatment did not significantly alter the levels (Figure 3C) or distribution (Figure 3A) of internalized mCherry-GluA1 subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Dynasore treatment reduced the levels of internalized TfR by 61% ± 6%.
source: Dynasore treatment reduced the levels of internalized TfR by 61% ± 6% (Figure 3D,E), consistent with endocytosis predominantly through clathrin-dependent endocytosis pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Dynasore treatment reduced internalized GluA1 subunits by only 10% ± 9%.
source: In contrast, dynasore treatment reduced internalized GluA1 subunits by only 10% ± 9% (Figure 3D,E), consistent with endocytosis predominantly through a different endocytosis pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by biotinylation assay data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: TC10 has a role in AMPAR recycling through an Arf6-dependent recycling pathway that is different from the TfR recycling pathway.
source: Based on these results together with previous data (Figure 2), we conclude that TC10 has a role in AMPAR recycling through an Arf6-dependent recycling pathway that is different from the TfR recycling pathway.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the dynasore experiments and the Arf6 co-localization data.

claim: Evidence that AMPARs are in REs and clathrin-coated pits comes almost exclusively from studies examining AMPAR activity-dependent recycling.
source: Evidence that AMPARs are in REs and clathrin-coated pits comes almost exclusively from studies examining AMPAR activity-dependent recycling.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the literature in the field.

claim: Chemically inducing LTP (cLTP) with glycine stimulation to activate synaptic NMDARs increased the AMPAR surface/total ratio by 39% ± 10%.
source: Chemically inducing LTP (cLTP) with glycine stimulation to activate synaptic NMDARs increased the AMPAR surface/total ratio by 39% ± 10% (p < 0.1, n = 10, 14)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring surface/total ratios after cLTP.

claim: Chemically inducing LTD (cLTD) with acute NMDA treatment decreased the AMPAR surface/total ratio by 62% ± 3%.
source: while chemically inducing LTD (cLTD) with acute NMDA treatment, decreased the AMPAR surface/total ratio by 62% ± 3% (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Neurons expressing TC10DN or TC10CA showed increased AMPAR surface/total ratios with cLTP.
source: Neurons expressing TC10DN or TC10CA showed increased AMPAR surface/total ratios with cLTP (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The percent increase in surface AMPARs with cLTP was even larger than controls when TC10DN or TC10CA were expressed.
source: The percent increase in surface AMPARs was even larger than controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TC10DN or TC10CA expression had no negative effect on cLTP-induced increases but reduced surface AMPAR levels prior to cLTP, consistent with AMPAR recycling occurring through multiple endocytosis pathways.
source: The finding that TC10DN or TC10CA expression had no negative effect on cLTP-induced increases but reduced surface AMPAR levels prior to cLTP is again consistent with AMPAR recycling occurring through multiple endocytosis pathways, one pathway providing AMPARs inserted during cLTP and the other pathway primarily involved in constitutive AMPAR recycling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TC10 mutants on constitutive vs. LTP conditions.

claim: In neurons expressing TC10 mutants during cLTD, only half the cLTD-induced decrease in AMPARs was observed with TC10DN, while TC10CA did not alter the cLTD-induced decrease.
source: In neurons expressing TC10 mutants during cLTD, we observed only half the cLTD-induced decrease in AMPARs with TC10DN, while TC10CA did not alter the cLTD-induced decrease (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: During LTD induced by low-frequency synaptic stimulation, AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents were reduced by 52.4% ± 0.5%.
source: Similar to what we observed with cLTD, the AMPAR-mediated synaptic currents were reduced by 52.4% ± 0.5% by LTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: During LTD, AMPAR EPSCs were reduced by 27.5% ± 1.0% in the presence of TC10DN.
source: During LTD, AMPAR EPSCs were reduced by 27.5% ± 1.0% in the presence of TC10DN, and TC10CA had no effect on LTD (a 48.3% ± 1.0% reduction) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TC10CA had no effect on LTD (a 48.3% ± 1.0% reduction).
source: During LTD, AMPAR EPSCs were reduced by 27.5% ± 1.0% in the presence of TC10DN, and TC10CA had no effect on LTD (a 48.3% ± 1.0% reduction) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 21% ± 2% of the internalized AMPARs co-localized with TfR under constitutive conditions.
source: We observed that 21% ± 2% of the internalized AMPARs co-localized with TfR (Figure 4D,E), consistent with a previous estimate of the amount of internalized AMPARs that co-localized with TfR during constitutive recycling (Park et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4D,E and citation to Park et al. (2004).

claim: 52% of the internalized AMPAR co-localized with Arf6-HA under constitutive conditions.
source: 52% of the internalized AMPAR co-localized with Arf6-HA
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization measurements.

claim: 27% of internalized AMPARs did not co-localize with TfRs or with Arf6-HA under constitutive conditions.
source: and 27% of internalized AMPARs did not co-localize with TfRs or with Arf6-HA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The pool of internalized AMPARs that did not co-localize with TfRs or Arf6-HA is likely in a different endosomal pool such as early endosomes, late endosomes, or lysosomes.
source: This pool of internalized AMPARs is likely in a different endosomal pool such as early endosomes, late endosomes, or lysosomes (Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data and supported by citation to Fernández-Monreal et al. (2012).

claim: After cLTP induction, cLTP increased the amount of internalized GluA1 that co-localized with TfR from 21% to 56%.
source: After cLTP induction, the distribution of internalized AMPARs in the different pools changed: cLTP increased the amount of internalized GluA1 that co-localized with TfR from 21% to 56% (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After cLTP, the internalized GluA1 that co-localized with Arf6 was unchanged (52% vs 47%).
source: while the internalized GluA1 that co-localized with Arf6 was unchanged (52% vs 47%; Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: cLTP increased the total amount of internalized GluA1 by 24% ± 5%.
source: cLTP increased the total amount of internalized GluA1 by 24% ± 5% (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After cLTP, the pool of internalized AMPARs that did not co-localize with TfRs or with Arf6-HA was no longer measurable.
source: while the pool of internalized AMPARs that did not co-localize with TfRs or with Arf6-HA was no longer measurable.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization measurements after cLTP.

claim: During constitutive recycling, AMPARs appear to be recycling primarily through a dynamin-independent, Arf6-, and TC10-dependent pathway though some recycle through a dynamin-dependent, TfR-containing pathway.
source: Our results are consistent with significant changes in AMPAR endocytosis and recycling that occurs during cLTP. During constitutive recycling, AMPARs appear to be recycling primarily through a dynamin-independent, Arf6-, and TC10-dependent pathway though some recycle through a dynamin-dependent, TfR-containing pathway.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the co-localization and dynasore experiments.

claim: After cLTP, a much larger fraction of the AMPARs recycle through the dynamin-dependent pathway taken by TfRs.
source: After cLTP, a much larger fraction of the AMPARs recycle through the dynamin-dependent pathway taken by TfRs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increased co-localization of internalized AMPARs with TfR after cLTP.

claim: After LTP, fewer AMPARs are trafficked for degradation via a late endosomal/lysosomal pathway.
source: Our results further suggest that after LTP, fewer AMPARs are trafficked for degradation via a late endosomal/lysosomal pathway as previously described (Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the disappearance of the pool of internalized AMPARs not co-localizing with TfR or Arf6 after cLTP, and supported by citation to Fernández-Monreal et al. (2012).

claim: Constitutive AMPAR recycling occurs largely through a pathway different from the clathrin-dependent pathway used by TfRs.
source: The findings of this study are consistent with constitutive AMPAR recycling occurring largely through a pathway different from the clathrin-dependent pathway used by TfRs.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the study.

claim: The features of the alternative AMPAR recycling pathway, for example, presence of Arf6 and independence from dynamin function, are consistent with a clathrin-independent endocytosis pathway.
source: The features of the alternative AMPAR recycling pathway, for example, presence of Arf6 and independence from dynamin function, are consistent with a clathrin-independent endocytosis pathway (Doherty and McMahon, 2009; Donaldson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to Doherty and McMahon (2009) and Donaldson et al. (2009).

claim: The Arf6-mediated, clathrin-independent pathway is a separate endocytosis pathway that exists in neurons and mediates the endocytosis and recycling of a number of different receptors and transport proteins.
source: The Arf6-mediated, clathrin-independent pathway is a separate endocytosis pathway that exists in neurons and mediates the endocytosis and recycling of a number of different receptors and transport proteins.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about the Arf6 pathway.

claim: The Arf6-mediated pathway mediates endocytosis and recycling of metabotropic glutamate receptors mGluR5 and mGluR7, and the potassium channel Kir3.4.
source: These include the metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR), mGluR5 (Fourgeaud et al., 2003) and mGluR7 (Lavezzari and Roche, 2007), and the potassium channel Kir3.4 (Gong et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fourgeaud et al. (2003), Lavezzari and Roche (2007), and Gong et al. (2007).

claim: AMPARs were shown to undergo a clathrin-independent recycling pathway, in addition to clathrin-mediated pathway in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: AMPARs were shown to undergo a clathrin-independent recycling pathway, in addition to clathrin-mediated pathway in Caenorhabditis elegans (Glodowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Glodowski et al. (2007).

claim: An EM study found that all intracellular structures with the features of REs were labeled for TfRs in dendritic shafts of cultured rat hippocampal neurons but only 28% of these REs were labeled for AMPARs.
source: Another study using electron microscopy (EM) (Tao-Cheng et al., 2011) also suggests that constitutive AMPAR recycling occurs through a different pathway. The study found that all intracellular structures with the features of REs were labeled for TfRs in dendritic shafts of cultured rat hippocampal neurons but only 28% of these REs were labeled for AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tao-Cheng et al. (2011).

claim: EM studies assaying AMPAR subunit localization in clathrin-coated pits observed few AMPARs in clathrin-coated pits.
source: EM studies assaying AMPAR subunit localization in clathrin-coated pits observed few AMPARs in clathrin-coated pits (Petralia et al., 2003; Tao-Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Petralia et al. (2003) and Tao-Cheng et al. (2011).

claim: Tao-Cheng et al. found that 76% of the clathrin-coated pits contained TfRs but only 24% of the pits contained AMPAR subunits.
source: Tao-Cheng et al. found that 76% of the clathrin-coated pits contained TfRs but only 24% of the pits contained AMPAR subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tao-Cheng et al.

claim: Clathrin-coated pits near PSDs have been proposed to be specialized endocytic zones (EZs) that mediate endocytosis of AMPA receptors for local recycling in spines.
source: Clathrin-coated pits near PSDs have been proposed to be specialized endocytic zones (EZs) (Blanpied et al., 2002; Racz et al., 2004) that mediate endocytosis of AMPA receptors for local recycling in spines (Lu et al., 2007; Petrini et al., 2009; Kennedy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Both EM studies failed to detect any AMPAR labeling in the EZs at synapses under conditions where constitutive AMPAR recycling was occurring.
source: Both EM studies failed to detect any AMPAR labeling in the EZs at synapses under conditions where constitutive AMPAR recycling was occurring (Petralia et al., 2003; Tao-Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Petralia et al. (2003) and Tao-Cheng et al. (2011).

claim: A previous study suggested that the associations between TC10 and AMPARs are indirect, requiring an adaptor protein, nPIST, which interacts with the AMPAR TARP subunit.
source: Results from a previous study suggest that the associations between TC10 and AMPARs are indirect, requiring an adaptor protein, nPIST, which interacts with the AMPAR TARP subunit (Cuadra et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cuadra et al. (2004).

claim: nPIST, like TC10, primarily co-localizes with Golgi markers in the somata of cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: nPIST, like TC10, primarily co-localizes with Golgi markers in the somata of cultured hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This claim draws from knowledge of nPIST localization.

claim: nPIST is also found in puncta in dendritic shafts, not in spines, and the puncta do not co-localize with Golgi membranes.
source: But it is also found in puncta in dendritic shafts, not in spines, and the puncta do not co-localize with Golgi membranes (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al. (2012).

claim: nPIST interactions with TC10 in dendrites are likely at the Arf6 endosomes where most of TC10 was observed in dendrites.
source: nPIST interactions with TC10 in dendrites, thus, are likely at the Arf6 endosomes where we observed most of TC10 in dendrites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data and knowledge of nPIST distribution.

claim: TC10 acts to regulate interactions between nPIST and AMPAR TARP subunits when present together in Arf6 endosomes, and thereby, regulate the trafficking of AMPARs from Arf6 endosomes to dendritic exocytosis sites.
source: One possibility is that TC10 acts to regulate interactions between nPIST and AMPAR TARP subunits when present together in Arf6 endosomes, and thereby, regulate the trafficking of AMPARs from Arf6 endosomes to dendritic exocytosis sites.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for TC10 function.

claim: The increase in AMPARs in REs after cLTP reflects a redistribution of trafficking AMPARs in dendrites such that AMPAR receptor recycling via REs is increased, while recycling via the Arf6-TC10-containing endosomes was unchanged.
source: The increase in AMPARs in REs after cLTP reflects a redistribution of trafficking AMPARs in dendrites such that AMPAR receptor recycling via REs is increased, while recycling via the Arf6-TC10-containing endosomes was unchanged.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data after cLTP.

claim: A previous study suggested that during LTD an activity-dependent switch occurs such that more endocytosed AMPARs in early endosomes were routed to the Rab7-dependent pathway to lysosomes and less were routed to the recycling endosome pathway.
source: A previous study suggested that during LTD an activity-dependent switch occurs such that more endocytosed AMPARs in early endosomes were routed to the Rab7-dependent pathway to lysosomes and less were routed to the recycling endosome pathway (Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fernández-Monreal et al. (2012).

claim: During cLTP, an activity-dependent switch occurs such that few to none of the endocytosed AMPARs in early endosomes are routed via the Rab7-dependent pathway to lysosomes, and virtually all AMPARs in early endosomes are routed to the REs.
source: Our data suggest that the opposite is occurring during cLTP. That is, an activity-dependent switch occurs such that few to none of the endocytosed AMPARs in early endosomes are routed via the Rab7-dependent pathway to lysosomes. Instead, virtually all AMPARs in early endosomes are routed to the REs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the pool of internalized AMPARs not co-localizing with TfR or Arf6 disappears after cLTP.

claim: Part of the increase in AMPARs in REs during cLTP appears to be caused by an increase in AMPAR endocytosis, presumably at clathrin-coated pits.
source: However, this switch can only explain part of the increase in AMPARs in REs during cLTP because the total number of endocytosed AMPARs increased by an additional 24%. Thus, part of the increase in AMPARs in REs during cLTP appears to be caused by an increase in AMPAR endocytosis, presumably at clathrin-coated pits
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that total internalized AMPARs increased by 24% after cLTP.

claim: Previous studies have found that synaptic stimulation increases dynamin- and clathrin-dependent AMPAR endocytosis.
source: Previous studies have found that synaptic stimulation increases dynamin- and clathrin-dependent AMPAR endocytosis (Carroll et al., 1999; Lüscher et al., 1999; Ehlers, 2000; Lee et al., 2002; Scholz et al., 2010; Tao-Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In some studies, blocking dynamin/clathrin-dependent endocytosis prevented LTD but did not alter constitutive AMPAR endocytosis.
source: In some of these studies, blocking dynamin/clathrin-dependent endocytosis prevented LTD but did not alter constitutive AMPAR endocytosis.
evidence: This claim draws from knowledge of previous studies.

claim: Blocking constitutive AMPAR endocytosis by interfering with NSF binding to GluA2 subunits does not alter LTD or activity-dependent AMPAR endocytosis.
source: It was also found that blocking constitutive AMPAR endocytosis by interfering with NSF binding to GluA2 subunits does not alter LTD or activity-dependent AMPAR endocytosis (Carroll et al., 1999; Lüscher et al., 1999; Ehlers, 2000; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: These studies demonstrate that activity-dependent and constitutive AMPAR recycling can be uncoupled, and thus, appears to be independently regulated, consistent with separate processes underlying activity-dependent and constitutive AMPAR recycling.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that activity-dependent and constitutive AMPAR recycling can be uncoupled, and thus, appears to be independently regulated, consistent with separate processes underlying activity-dependent and constitutive AMPAR recycling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies showing differential regulation of the two types of recycling.

claim: The two different AMPAR recycling pathways serve different functions.
source: The results from this study suggest that the two different AMPAR recycling pathways serve different functions.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the study.

claim: The Arf6-dependent recycling pathway, also dependent on TC10 function, predominates during AMPAR constitutive recycling.
source: The Arf6-dependent recycling pathway, also dependent on TC10 function, predominates during AMPAR constitutive recycling.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing high co-localization with Arf6 and effects of TC10 mutants under constitutive conditions.

claim: Another recycling pathway, which is dynamin and clathrin dependent, increases during AMPAR activity-dependent recycling (cLTP and cLTD).
source: Another recycling pathway, which is dynamin and clathrin dependent, increases during AMPAR activity-dependent recycling (cLTP and cLTD).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased co-localization with TfR after cLTP.

claim: The two recycling pathways originate at separate endocytosis sites, either clathrin-coated pits or clathrin-independent sites.
source: To explain the effects of dynamin inhibition, we propose that the two recycling pathways originate at separate endocytosis sites, either clathrin-coated pits or clathrin-independent sites.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The two recycling pathways merge at early endosomes, where AMPARs would be sorted for trafficking into the various pools.
source: As proposed by others (Donaldson et al., 2009) but not shown in the model, the two recycling pathways merge at early endosomes, where AMPARs would be sorted for trafficking into the various pools, either the REs used by TfRs, the Arf6-depedent REs or late endosomes for lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference and citation to Donaldson et al. (2009).

claim: The two recycling pathways end when AMPARs are exocytosed at separate sites at the cell membrane.
source: As proposed in the model, the two recycling pathways end when AMPARs are exocytosed at separate sites at the cell membrane.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The presence of two different AMPAR recycling exocytosis sites may help to explain recent data describing different AMPAR recycling exocytosis sites.
source: The presence of two different AMPAR recycling exocytosis sites may help to explain recent data describing different AMPAR recycling exocytosis sites (Kennedy et al., 2010; Ahmad et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an explanation for observations in other studies, supported by citations to Kennedy et al. (2010) and Ahmad et al. (2012).

claim: The Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway has largely a caretaker role, delivering AMPARs to early endosomes where a decision is made to degrade internalized AMPARs or return them to the plasma membrane.
source: We envision that the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway has largely a caretaker role, delivering AMPARs to early endosomes where a decision is made to degrade internalized AMPARs or return them to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling functions predominantly during synaptic activation and appear to have a different role than the Arf6/TC10-depedent recycling pathway.
source: The dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling functions predominantly during synaptic activation and appear to have a different role than the Arf6/TC10-depedent recycling pathway (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and presented in the model in Figure 5.

claim: β2-adrenergic and M3 muscarinic receptors undergo constitutive recycling when not activated by ligand via an Arf6-dependent, clathrin-independent pathway, and after ligand activation, their recycling pathway switches to the clathrin-dependent pathway.
source: Other receptors are regulated in a similar way by the same two recycling pathways. β2-adrenergic and M3 muscarinic receptors undergo constitutive recycling when not activated by ligand via an Arf6-dependent, clathrin-independent pathway. After ligand activation, their recycling pathway switches and recycling occurs via the clathrin-dependent pathway (Scarselli and Donaldson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scarselli and Donaldson (2009).

claim: The recycling pathway of α1-integrin receptors also switches after their activation.
source: The recycling pathway of α1-integrin receptors also switches after their activation (Arjonen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arjonen et al. (2012).

claim: Increases in synaptic AMPARs during NMDAR-dependent LTP were previously thought to increase AMPAR exocytosis without increasing AMPAR endocytosis causing a decrease in the level of AMPARs in REs.
source: Previously, it was assumed that AMPAR recycling was largely confined to a single synaptic spine and the dendrite area nearby (Figure 5A). Increases in synaptic AMPARs during NMDAR-dependent LTP were thought to increase AMPAR exocytosis without increasing AMPAR endocytosis causing a decrease in the level of AMPARs in REs (Malinow and Malenka, 2002; Bredt and Nicoll, 2003; Collingridge et al., 2004; Park et al., 2004; Shepherd and Huganir, 2007).
evidence: This claim describes the prevailing assumption in the field, supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: AMPAR levels in REs increased after LTP, and endocytosis increased in parallel with increased AMPAR levels at synapses during cLTP.
source: However, we found that AMPAR levels in REs increased after LTP, and endocytosis increased in parallel with increased AMPAR levels at synapses during cLTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased co-localization with TfR and increased total internalized AMPARs after cLTP.

claim: AMPAR recycling is not limited to trafficking AMPARs into and out of the same synaptic spine.
source: Our results suggest that AMPAR recycling is not limited to trafficking AMPARs into and out of the same synaptic spine.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that AMPAR endocytosis increases during cLTP.

claim: AMPAR recycling has the additional function of transporting AMPARs to sites distant from where they originate.
source: Instead, we suggest that AMPAR recycling has the additional function of transporting AMPARs to sites distant from where they originate.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Increased AMPAR endocytosis during cLTP occurs through the dynamin-dependent recycling pathway starting at clathrin-coated pits at sites distant from synapses undergoing cLTP.
source: Increased AMPAR endocytosis during cLTP occurs through the dynamin-dependent recycling pathway starting at clathrin-coated pits at sites distant from synapses undergoing cLTP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data and presented in Figure 5C.

claim: AMPARs were not found in clathrin-coated pits at spines but in clathrin-coated pits well outside spines along the dendritic shafts.
source: Consistent with this idea, AMPARs were not found in clathrin-coated pits at spines but in clathrin-coated pits well outside spines along the dendritic shafts (Tao-Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tao-Cheng et al. (2011).

claim: After endocytosis, AMPARs are trafficked in REs outside the synaptic spine region.
source: After endocytosis, we propose that AMPARs are trafficked in REs outside the synaptic spine region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference and presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Different kinds of endosomes, including REs, travel long distances to new locations during recycling in dendrites and axons.
source: Consistent with this trafficking role are studies demonstrating that different kinds of endosomes, including REs, travel long distances to new locations during recycling in dendrites and axons (Yap and Winckler, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yap and Winckler (2012).

claim: An EM study using three-dimensional reconstruction analysis found that in dendrites of rat hippocampal neurons independent REs were not maintained at each spine, and up to 20 spines shared a single recycling endosome.
source: Furthermore, an EM study using three-dimensional reconstruction analysis found that in dendrites of rat, hippocampal neurons independent REs were not maintained at each spine. Instead, up to 20 spines shared a single recycling endosome (Cooney et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cooney et al. (2002).

claim: The role for the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway during cLTP is to move AMPARs from sites distant from synaptic activation to sites near the activated synapse.
source: In short, we propose that the role for the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway during cLTP is to move AMPARs from sites distant from synaptic activation to sites near the activated synapse.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: During cLTD, AMPAR recycling via the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway is also increased similar to what occurs during cLTP, except recycling AMPARs in TfR-containing REs are trafficked in and out of synapses and along dendrites in the opposite direction.
source: During cLTD, we propose that AMPAR recycling via the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway is also increased similar to what occurs during cLTP. Recycling AMPARs in TfR-containing REs are trafficked in and out of synapses and along dendrites except in the opposite direction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference and presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Many studies have found that AMPAR endocytosis increases via the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway during LTD.
source: This is consistent with many studies that have found that AMPAR endocytosis increases via the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway.
evidence: This claim draws from knowledge of the literature in the field.

claim: It has been assumed that during LTD, increased AMPAR endocytosis occurs without increased AMPAR exocytosis resulting in larger local endosomal stores of AMPARs.
source: However, it has been assumed that during LTD, increased AMPAR endocytosis occurs without increased AMPAR exocytosis resulting in larger local endosomal stores of AMPARs.
evidence: This claim describes a prevailing assumption in the field.

claim: During cLTD, AMPARs are transported away from synapses.
source: Instead, we suggest that during cLTD, AMPARs are transported away from synapses.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Tao-Cheng et al. reported the appearance of AMPARs in clathrin-coated pits within synaptic spines during cLTD, which was not observed during constitutive conditions or cLTP.
source: In support of this idea, Tao-Cheng et al., (2011) reported the appearance of AMPARs in clathrin-coated pits within synaptic spines, which was not observed during constitutive conditions or cLTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tao-Cheng et al. (2011).

claim: AMPARs are trafficked during cLTD from clathrin-coated pits at activated spines via REs to distant sites.
source: In our model, AMPARs are trafficked during cLTD from clathrin-coated pits at activated spines via REs to distant sites.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: AMPARs flow out of synaptic spines during cLTD and into synaptic spines during cLTP.
source: Overall, AMPARs flow out of synaptic spines during cLTD and into synaptic spines during cLTP.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the proposed model.

claim: The function of the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway is to traffic AMPARs from regions of low activity to regions of high activity and in this way the pathway underlies a Hebbian redistribution of AMPARs.
source: The function of the dynamin/clathrin-dependent recycling pathway is, thus, to traffic AMPARs from regions of low activity to regions of high activity and in this way the pathway underlies a Hebbian redistribution of AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: TC10WT expression had opposite effects on synaptic AMPAR currents and the cell-surface levels of dendritic AMPARs, suggesting that the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway traffics AMPARs out of synaptic spines.
source: Our finding that TC10WT expression had opposite effects on synaptic AMPAR currents, a measure of functional synaptic AMPARs, and the cell-surface levels of dendritic AMPARs suggests that the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway traffics AMPARs out of synaptic spines.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TC10WT on synaptic vs. dendritic surface AMPARs.

claim: TC10WT expression increases exocytosis from Arf6-dependent pathway REs so that fewer AMPARs are in the Arf6 endosomes and more AMPARs are in the plasma membrane.
source: The simplest explanation for why TC10WT expression acts to increase cell-surface AMPARs levels is that it increases exocytosis from Arf6-dependent pathway REs so that fewer AMPARs are in the Arf6 endosomes and more AMPARs are in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is a proposed explanation based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The Arf6-dependent recycling pathway acts to traffic AMPARs via endocytosis and exocytosis from synapses to distant plasma membrane sites.
source: The decrease in the levels of synaptic AMPARs with TC10WT expression can be explained if the Arf6-dependent recycling pathway acts to traffic AMPARs via endocytosis and exocytosis from synapses to distant plasma membrane sites.
evidence: This claim is a proposed explanation based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: During constitutive AMPAR recycling, if AMPAR recycling via the Arf6-dependent recycling pathway acts to move synaptic AMPARs out of the spine and away from the synapse, then counteracting processes must be bringing other AMPARs back to the synapse in order to keep the levels of AMPAR constant.
source: During constitutive AMPAR recycling, if AMPAR recycling via the Arf6-dependent recycling pathway acts to move synaptic AMPARs out of the spine and away from the synapse, then counteracting processes must be bringing other AMPARs back to the synapse in order to keep the levels of AMPAR constant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed model to maintain homeostasis.

claim: During cLTD, the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway acts together with the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway to traffic AMPARs away from synaptic spines.
source: During cLTD (Figure 5D), we suggest that the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway acts together with the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway to traffic AMPARs away from synaptic spines.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference and presented in Figure 5D.

claim: If the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway traffics AMPARs out of the spines then blocking it would act to reduce LTD, as observed with TC10DN expression.
source: If the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway traffics AMPARs out of the spines then blocking it would act to reduce LTD, as we observed with TC10DN expression (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed model and the experimental observations with TC10DN.

claim: During constitutive conditions and during cLTP, the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway would act counter to the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway, which would traffic AMPARs into synaptic spines under these conditions.
source: During constitutive conditions (Figure 5B) and during cLTP (Figure 5C), the Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway would act counter to the dynamin/clathrin-dependent pathway, which in our model would traffic AMPARs into synaptic spines under these conditions.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference and presented in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Blocking Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway with the TC10DN expression may actually increase levels of LTP.
source: This aspect of our model explains why blocking Arf6/TC10-dependent recycling pathway with the TC10DN expression may actually increase levels of LTP (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed model and the experimental observations with TC10DN during cLTP.
